text: Verify succeeding proves the user controlled that address at the moment they signed. HTTP is stateless — a session is the missing piece that ties later requests back to that proven identity.

After verify succeeds, the backend writes the address into a session store and sets a cookie. Its advantage is real, immediate revocation — delete the session, and the user is logged out next request.
A JWT bakes the address and an expiry into a signed token, nothing stored server-side. It scales easily, but trades away real-time revocation — it's valid until it expires, full stop.

A Web3 session has two extra triggers beyond logout: a wallet disconnecting, and a wallet switching accounts. Miss the second one and requests can appear to come from a new account while still authorized as the old.
Verification happens once; a session, and its expiry, is what carries it forward safely. Lesson 24 closes the chapter with a different problem: letting users transact without holding ETH for gas.
